items.about:
I've spent most of my career inside planning processes that were technically correct and operationally irrelevant.

Good data. Solid models. And still, the decisions that mattered were made somewhere else.

That's the problem I keep coming back to.

Not how to build better forecasts. But how to make planning actually useful for the people who need to act on it. Customers don't experience your IBP cycle. They experience whether you showed up when it counted.

The organizations I've worked with that got this right had one thing in common. They stopped treating planning as an internal discipline and started treating it as a customer-facing capability.

That shift is harder than it sounds. It changes what you measure, who you involve, and what a good meeting looks like.

I've led that kind of change in global pharma and consumer goods environments. Not always cleanly. But consistently enough to know what works and what just looks like progress.

If that tension between planning sophistication and real customer impact is something you're navigating, I'd be glad to get into contact and exchange.

www.john-kloetzing.com

items.about:
Most manufacturers treat their supply chain like overhead. The ones I've worked with treat it like a weapon — and they win bids their competitors can't touch.
At Finish Thompson, our lead times were a quarter of our competitors'. We didn't just win on price. We won because we could promise delivery in two weeks when everyone else said eight. That one operational advantage contributed 32% in incremental revenue. The sales team got all the credit. (We let them.)
I do this now as a fractional CPO. I help mid-market manufacturers turn their supply chain into a revenue weapon. The sweet spot is $50M to $500M companies that are growing, not broken. The supply chain works. It just hasn't kept up with the business.
I've been doing this for 25 years, at companies worth $42M to $5.1B — GE Transportation, Visteon, Blue Bird, Finish Thompson, and others. I've managed up to $63M in annual supplier spend. Some of what that's looked like:
• 32% revenue growth from cutting lead times from eight weeks to two
• 98.7% inventory availability through COVID, while competitors went on allocation
• 121 products reshored from China. Zero stoppages, 12% net cheaper.
• $8.6M emergency supplier takeover, on time and on budget
• 4.6% cost reduction across top vendors, without switching a single one
• $50M six-year contract with $5.9M in scheduled reductions built in
• $150M+ in supplier contracts negotiated over the career
Most $50M to $500M manufacturers don't need a full-time CPO. They need CPO-level thinking on their three or four most critical problems, from someone who's solved them before. You get the strategy at a fraction of the cost, with results in the first 90 days. Not the first 90 days of a job search.
I take on a limited number of engagements at a time. Right now I have room for a few more. If your supply chain is a sales obstacle when it should be a sales weapon, let's talk. No deck, no pitch. Just an honest 30-minute conversation about what's actually going on.

items.about:
My professional plan was to become a college professor, sharing my love of English literature written before 1700 with new generations of students. Shakespeare, Chaucer, and Milton were my favorites.

Along the way, that plan was completely shuffled by circumstances beyond my control. And yet what seemed to be going wrong at the time, ended up going very right.

I’m still applying my love of reading and writing, but in a very different space – procurement and supply chain. My learning journey started at the corporate headquarters of a large grocery retailer, wound through the consulting team at a software provider, and then led me to be a very unlikely entrepreneur. 

Every step of the way, I’ve built on a core set of skills by adding new approaches, relationships, and ideas to my toolkit. Each question starting with, “Have you ever considered…” was a new potential doorway to walk through. 

Not every leg of my journey has been successful, but I never stopped moving forward either. I’ve learned far more from my mistakes than I have from my successes (although those successes definitely help dull the pain!)

I’m still leaning on my ability to read and write and the sheer joy I find in working with others as I expand into new types of content creation, and as my confidence continues to grow, so does the length of my journey. 

If you see anything in my past or present that is of interest to you, reach out and let’s connect!
